claims.text: Tempered martensitic steel can exhibit a ductile–brittle–ductile transition under a precisely controlled tempering protocol.
The transition is caused by temperature-activated impurity segregation at intermediate temperatures followed by impurity redistribution at higher temperatures.
The initial material is an as-quenched tempered martensitic steel.
The initial microstructure is primed for transformation during heat treatment.
Heating the steel into a narrow temper-embrittlement window activates impurity segregation.
Continued heating beyond the embrittlement window reverses or redistributes the segregated impurities.
Phosphorus and sulfur can segregate to grain boundaries during tempering.
Grain-boundary impurity segregation at intermediate temperatures causes a marked loss of ductility.
Further heating promotes impurity diffusion and redistribution.
Redistribution of grain-boundary impurities alleviates embrittlement and restores ductility.
Ductility will transiently decrease at specific tempering temperatures.
Ductility will recover after heating sufficiently beyond the embrittlement window.
The proposed behavior occurs only within a limited temperature window.
Departures from optimal alloy composition or treatment parameters may prevent the transition.
Compositionally complex and high-entropy alloys are not expected to exhibit the proposed ductile–brittle–ductile transition.
The relevant temperature range and magnitude of ductility change depend on alloy composition and heat-treatment protocol.

contradictions.description: The initial and baseline material is called both 'as-quenched' and 'tempered.' As-quenched ordinarily denotes the state before tempering, whereas tempered denotes a subsequent heat-treated state, leaving the starting condition internally ambiguous.
